finding.claim: Missing authorization on DELETE: `require_allowed` is an alias of `acl.is_allowed`, which only returns a bool. The result is discarded, so any caller can delete any file. The name suggests it enforces the check, but only `ensure_allowed` aborts.
finding.source: Any HTTP client sending DELETE /files/<fid>, with any or no X-Session-User-Verified header, and a valid fid.

trace.note: `from acl import is_allowed as require_allowed` aliases the non-enforcing boolean function
f = STORE[fid] looks up the resource by the attacker-supplied id
require_allowed(...) returns False but the value is ignored, so no abort(403)
is_allowed returns a bool and never aborts

finding.guards_checked: The only authorization call is the ignored is_allowed. There is no decorator, no other before_request check (load_user only sets g.user), and no try/except. The rename route uses ensure_allowed correctly, which confirms the delete route is the outlier.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: the only check is require_allowed, an alias of the boolean is_allowed whose result is discarded; the before_request hook load_user only sets g.user, and there is no decorator or try/except.
verdict.reason: views.py:4 aliases the boolean acl.is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) as require_allowed, views.py:18 calls it as a bare statement that never aborts, so views.py:19 `del STORE[fid]` runs for any unauthenticated caller, unlike rename_file which uses ensure_allowed at views.py:26.

finding.claim: Authentication is a client-supplied header. g.user is taken straight from `X-Session-User-Verified` with no session, signature or token validation. Unless a trusted proxy strips and sets this header, anyone can impersonate any user, including a user holding write grants, and pass the ACL checks.
finding.source: The attacker-controlled request header `X-Session-User-Verified: <victim user id>`.
finding.sink: The ACL check `ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "write")` in rename_file, and the protected rename `f["name"] = ...`.

trace.note: The grants lookup is keyed by the spoofed user string, so the check passes for a victim with grants

finding.guards_checked: No signature, session or HMAC verification exists in this code. There is no evidence in the repo of an upstream proxy that strips the header; the "Verified" name only implies one. This is a precondition-dependent finding: it is exploitable if the app is reachable directly or the proxy does not strip the header.

verdict.guard_found: ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts 403 correctly, but it only checks grants keyed by the attacker-supplied user string; no signature/session validation and no proxy header-stripping in the repo.
verdict.reason: views.py:12 sets g.user directly from the client header, and views.py:26 passes it to ensure_allowed, which (acl.py:5,9-10) only looks up grants by that string, so spoofing a granted user passes the check and views.py:27 renames the file; this depends on no upstream proxy stripping the header, which can't be seen in the repo.

finding.claim: Unhandled lookups and input errors. `STORE[fid]` raises KeyError and `request.json["name"]` raises on a missing or non-JSON body, both producing 500s. Because the lookup happens before the authz check, this also leaks which file ids exist (500 vs 403) to unauthorized users. The impact is low.
finding.source: The fid path parameter and the JSON body.
finding.sink: STORE[fid] lookup and the 500 error response, which acts as an existence oracle.

trace.note: STORE[fid] is accessed before any authorization
The same pattern appears in rename_file

finding.guards_checked: There is no error handler and no authorization before the lookup. The impact is limited to information disclosure and a minor availability effect.

verdict.guard_found: No error handler and no existence check before the lookup. `ensure_allowed` (acl.py:8-10) aborts 403 but runs only after `STORE[fid]`. In delete_file, `require_allowed` is an alias for the bool-returning `is_allowed` and its result is discarded (views.py:18).
verdict.reason: views.py:25 does `STORE[fid]` before `ensure_allowed` at views.py:26, so a missing id gives a 500 and an existing but unauthorized id gives a 403 (acl.py:10), which is an existence oracle; views.py:27 `request.json["name"]` is also unvalidated; the impact is low, as the finding says.
